title: Chickpea chopped salad + vinaigrette
skill: Whisking a vinaigrette, dressing to taste

notes.text: For more than 8, toss the salad in two bowls, with half the dressing in each, so the bottom doesn't get crushed.

move.title: Chop it small, whisk it smooth
move.body: A chopped salad has everything cut to about the size of a chickpea, so every forkful has a bit of all of it. Today you'll cut five vegetables into small, even pieces, whisk a red wine vinaigrette from scratch, and taste it on a lettuce leaf until it's just right.

callback.body: In the Caesar, the mayonnaise held the dressing together. A vinaigrette has no mayonnaise, so a spoon of mustard does that job, and the oil goes in slowly while you whisk.

why.title: Chickpea-size pieces
why.body: When the cucumber, tomato, pepper, and lettuce are all about as big as a chickpea, they mix evenly and fit on a fork together. One big chunk of cucumber would crowd everything else off.

why.title: Three spoons of oil to one of vinegar
why.body: Vinegar is sour and sharp. Oil is smooth and mild. About three parts oil to one part vinegar balances them, so the dressing tastes bright without making you pucker. It's a starting point: taste, then fix it.

why.title: Mustard holds it together
why.body: Oil and vinegar don't mix on their own; shake them and they split again in a minute. Mustard has tiny bits in it that grab onto oil on one side and vinegar on the other, so whisked with the mustard, the oil breaks into little drops that stay spread through the vinegar.

why.title: Slowly, while you whisk
why.body: Pour the oil all at once and it sits on top in a puddle. A thin stream, whisked in as it goes, breaks into drops small enough for the mustard to hold.

why.title: Cold water tames the onion
why.body: Raw red onion can taste sharp and stay with you all day. A few minutes in cold water washes off the juice that bites, and the onion stays crunchy and sweet.

why.title: Dress it right before eating
why.body: The salt and vinegar in a dressing pull water out of cut vegetables and wilt lettuce. Tossed just before eating, the salad stays crisp. Leftover salad keeps better with the dressing on the side.

wrong.sign: The dressing tastes so sour it makes you pucker
wrong.fix: Whisk in a little more oil, or a tiny bit of honey, then taste again on a leaf.

wrong.sign: The dressing tastes flat and oily
wrong.fix: Add a pinch of salt and a teaspoon of vinegar, whisk, and taste again.

wrong.sign: The dressing split into oil and vinegar
wrong.fix: Whisk hard for 20 seconds right before you pour it. It's normal for a vinaigrette to split a little as it sits.

wrong.sign: The salad is watery at the bottom of the bowl
wrong.fix: It sat too long after dressing, or the lettuce was wet. Next time, dry the leaves well and toss just before eating.

quiz.q: About how much oil goes with 1 spoon of vinegar?
quiz.explain: Three to one is the starting point. Then taste and fix it.

quiz.q: What does the mustard do in a vinaigrette?
choices: Helps the oil and vinegar stay mixed
quiz.explain: It holds the little drops of oil in the vinegar.

quiz.q: How do you add the oil?
choices: In a thin stream while you whisk
quiz.explain: Slowly, so it breaks into small drops.

quiz.q: When do you pour the dressing on?
quiz.explain: Dressing wilts lettuce and pulls water from the vegetables.

steps.text: Pull the romaine leaves apart and rinse them in the colander with the cucumber, tomatoes, and pepper. Roll the leaves in the kitchen towel and press until they're dry.
steps.tip: Dry leaves hold the dressing. Wet ones make it run off.

steps.text: Open the chickpeas, drain them in the colander, and rinse them under cold water. Put them in the large bowl.
steps.tip: Keep your fingers away from the edge of the lid.

steps.text: Peel the onion half. Cut it into thin slices, then cut across the slices to chop it small. Put it in the small bowl and cover it with cold water.
steps.tip: Hold the onion with your hand shaped like a claw, fingertips tucked in.

steps.text: Cut the ends off the cucumber and cut it into 3 pieces. Cut each piece into planks, the planks into sticks, and the sticks into small cubes. Add them to the bowl.
steps.look: Cubes about as big as a chickpea.

steps.text: Cut each tomato in half and cut out the hard core. Cut the halves into strips, then across into small cubes. Add them to the bowl.
steps.tip: Lay the tomato cut side down so it can't roll.

steps.text: Stand the pepper on its end and cut the four sides off the core. Lay each piece skin side down, cut it into strips, then across into small squares. Add them to the bowl.
steps.look: Pieces about the same size as the cucumber.

steps.text: Stack a few romaine leaves, cut them the long way into strips about ½ inch wide, then cut across the strips. Put the lettuce in the medium bowl, apart from the rest.
steps.tip: The lettuce waits on its own so it stays crisp.

steps.text: Peel the garlic and mince it into tiny bits.
Pour the onion into the colander to drain. In the small bowl, whisk the garlic, vinegar, mustard, honey, oregano, salt, and pepper together.
Keep whisking while you pour in the olive oil in a thin stream, a little at a time, until it's all in.
steps.look: Cloudy and a little thick, with no puddle of oil on top.
steps.tip: Set the bowl on a damp towel so it doesn't spin while you whisk.

steps.text: Dip a piece of lettuce in the dressing and taste it. Too sour? Whisk in a little more oil. Flat? Add a pinch of salt. Taste again until you like it.
steps.tip: Taste on a leaf, not a spoon. That's how you'll eat it.

steps.text: Right before eating, add the lettuce and the drained onion to the big bowl. Whisk the dressing again, pour on about two thirds of it, and toss until everything is coated. Add more if you like, and top with the feta if you're using it.
steps.tip: Leftover dressing keeps in a jar in the fridge for a week. Shake it before you use it.

wash.text: Separate and rinse the romaine with the cucumber, tomatoes, and pepper, and dry the leaves completely in the towel. Set out the board, the knife, and the bowls, and note the time: the knife work, from the onion to the garlic, is this week's mastery check.
wash.tip: Even first, fast second. Every cube the same size matters more than the clock.

onion.text: Peel the onion half, leaving the root on, and mince it: strips ⅛ inch apart toward the root, then across at ⅛ inch. Soak it in the small bowl of cold water while you cut the rest.

cucumber.text: Trim the cucumber and cut it into 3-inch pieces. Cut ¼-inch planks, ¼-inch sticks, then ¼-inch cubes. Add them to the chickpeas.
cucumber.look: ¼-inch cubes, close to the same size.

tomatoes.text: Core the tomatoes, halve them, and cut them into ¼-inch cubes, cut side down. Add them to the bowl.
tomatoes.look: ¼-inch cubes, the same size as the cucumber.

pepper.text: Cut the sides off the pepper, trim the ribs, and cut it skin side down into ¼-inch strips, then ¼-inch squares. Add them to the bowl.

lettuce.text: Cut the romaine into ½-inch ribbons, then across into ½-inch squares. Keep it in the medium bowl, apart from the rest.

garlic.text: Mince the garlic. Check the time: that's your knife-work time for this week.

dressing.text: Drain the onion. Whisk the garlic, vinegar, mustard, honey, oregano, salt, and pepper in the small bowl.

oil.text: Whisk in the oil in a thin stream until it's all in and the dressing is cloudy and smooth.

taste.text: Taste the dressing on a lettuce leaf and balance it: more oil if it's sharp, salt if it's flat, vinegar if it's dull and oily. Write down what you added.

toss.text: Right before serving, add the lettuce and onion, whisk the dressing again, and toss the salad with about two thirds of it. Add more to taste, and top with feta if you're using it.
